To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
CC2D proteins regulate the budding of human immunodeficient virus type 1 by binding to and regulating the function of ESCRT III proteins.
CC2DIA and CC2DIB bind to CHMP4 proteins and regulate their polymerization and HIV-1 budding activity.
CC2D proteins are novel regulators of CHMP4 function in HIV-1 release.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of a novel regulator of CHMP4 function in HIV-1 release.
the first description of a novel class of ESCRT-associated proteins and with the first evidence that CHMP4 proteins can be sequestered by other proteins.
a previously unrecognized regulatory pathway for the ESCRT pathway and HIV-1 budding.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CC2D proteins are novel regulators of CHMP4 function in HIV-1 release.
CC2D proteins are involved in HIV budding, and this is a novel and interesting observation.
CC2D proteins regulate HIV-1 budding by sequestering CHMP4s and by an as-yet-undetermined mechanism that is independent of this interaction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CC2D proteins are novel regulators of the CHMP4-ESCRTIII machinery that may be involved in the budding of other viruses and possibly also in the budding of cellular membranes.
CC2D proteins act as CHMP4 regulators that modulate the release of HIV-1.
the CHMP4/CC2D1A/ALIX complex is a key regulator of ESCRT-III function in HIV-1 egress.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the budding of HIV-1 and perhaps other viruses is regulated by the sequestration of late-acting ESCRT components.
